Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand and
popular perception suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate
student growth is not synonymous with understanding student growth:
– The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple
to understand conceptually.
– Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult to
calculate but are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple
conceptual basis.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

• There are 3 general approaches of calculating student growth:
– Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
– Growth as a norm/peer referenced quantity.
– Growth as a criterion referenced quantity.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• Growth as an amount of change:
– What could be more simple?
– Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
– Requires a vertical scale (which Indiana had up to 2014/ISTEP+)
– Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1
• Not as simple as it seems:
– Comparisons between students often leads to wrong
conclusions
– Interpreting change requires context.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

•This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
•Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
•Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to acquire that context.

An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age
and is shown to have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of
increase—4 inches—is a well understood quantity that any
parent can grasp and calculate at home using a simple
yardstick. However, parents leaving their pediatrician’s office
knowing only how much their child has grown would likely be
wanting for more information: Parents are not interested in an
absolute magnitude of growth, but instead in a norm-
referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase alongside the
height increases of similar children.

HISTORY OF STUDENT GROWTH IN INDIANA

• Started under Wes Bruce in 2008 with the Rooney Foundation.

• Included the calculation of student growth percentiles and student
growth projections.

• Due to feedback from eld that they wanted to know in advance
what their growth goal was, Indiana began providing scale score
targets for typical and higher growth a year in advance.

• This “rolling baseline” approach used up to 2014-2015.

• Based upon the work of the student growth accountability work group, a new
model of student growth was adopted for the 2014-2015 academic year.

• Transitions of standards and assessments disrupts both status and growth
calculations.

• The “monkey wrench” with the new assessment is a different scale.

• The new scale doesn’t impact calculation of historical growth.

• The new scale does impact the calculation of growth-to-standard: Future
adequate growth.

2015-2016 STUDENT GROWTH IN INDIANA
• .Based upon the work of the accountability work group, a
criterion-referenced growth model was developed that blends
value-tables and observed growth.

• The model sub-divides Indiana’s 3 achievement levels into 8 sub-
achievement levels to determine starting ranges for students.

• Based upon observed student growth toward reaching/
maintaining passing status, points are given to students based
upon the progress made.

• School summaries are derived from individual student scores.

CONSIDERATIONS
• The current model is robust to changes in standards and assessments.
However, starting achievement levels and target ranges and points need to be
re-considered when transitions occur.

• Important to examine relationship between growth and relevant school
characteristics including:

• Average prior achievement.

• School poverty.

• Test mode effects have existed in the past and are a constant concern when
different test modes (e.g., online and paper-pencil).
